subject: Economy
theme: Debt sustainability and fiscal insolvency in countries
question_short_text: Definition of a country in debt trap condition
text: A country is said to be in debt trap if:
options: It has to abide by the conditionalities imposed by the International Monetary Fund
It has to borrow to make interest payments on outstanding loans
It has been refused loans or aid by creditors abroad
The World Bank charges a very high rate of interest on outstanding as well as new loans
answerText: (b) It has to borrow to make interest payments on outstanding loans
explanation: A debt trap occurs when a country's fiscal position deteriorates so severely that it must take on new borrowing simply to service (pay interest on) its existing debt. This creates an unsustainable spiral where debt grows faster than the country's capacity to repay it from economic output.

research.summary: The defining characteristic of a debt trap is not punitive lending terms, IMF conditionality, or being cut off from credit. Rather, it is the emergence of an unsustainable debt spiral where interest obligations themselves force a country into further borrowing. The trap works like this: if a country's government revenues and economic growth cannot cover the interest payments due on its debt stock, it must borrow new money to pay those interest costs. This new borrowing increases the total debt, which increases future interest obligations, creating a vicious cycle. The country's debt-to-GDP ratio rises not because of new productive investments, but because new loans are consumed entirely by servicing old debt. This is precisely why the question identifies option (b) as the core definition. Option (a) mentions IMF conditionality, which while restrictive and often controversial, is merely a consequence of debt distress, not its definition. Option (c) involves being excluded from credit markets, which represents a symptom or aftermath of debt crisis but is not the defining condition of being in a trap. Option (d) focuses on interest rate levels charged by the World Bank, but a high rate alone does not create the trap—the trap emerges when the country cannot afford those payments from its fiscal position and must refinance them. Historical examples like Sri Lanka (forced to take additional Chinese loans to service previous debts) and Laos (borrowing domestically to repay external debt) illustrate this mechanism. The trap is fundamentally about the contradiction between debt service obligations and fiscal capacity—when interest payments exceed what a country can pay from its own revenues and economic activity, perpetual new borrowing becomes inevitable, and true debt sustainability collapses.
facts: Debt service refers to the payment of both principal and interest on debt; when interest payments alone exceed government revenue capacity, debt sustainability is compromised

High debt-to-GDP ratios do not always indicate a debt trap—the critical factor is whether debt service obligations exceed the country's ability to generate primary surpluses (revenues minus non-interest spending)
The World Bank and IMF both assess debt sustainability using debt service ratios, defined as total debt service (interest plus principal) as a percentage of government revenues or exports

Countries like Zambia, Kenya, and others have entered debt distress precisely because rising interest rates on external debt created obligations they could not meet without new borrowing, forcing a refinancing squeeze
Debt trap conditions typically worsen during periods of currency depreciation or rising global interest rates, as these increase the real burden of servicing foreign-currency-denominated debt
